fields.text: Peas grow best in cool, moist conditions on a rich, well-structured loam with plenty of humus. Light soil can give an early crop and heavier soil a later one, but very poor soil gives disappointing yields.

Deeply cultivate the ground and prepare it well in autumn or winter. Incorporate plenty of compost or well-rotted manure where the soil lacks humus, but avoid heavy nitrogen dressings, which encourage leaf at the expense of pods.
Moisture is critical once plants are growing and especially while pods are filling. Soil rich in humus holds water better, and watering in dry spells usually pays back in extra peas.
After cropping, cut the plants at ground level and leave the roots in the soil so the nitrogen-rich nodules remain available to following crops.

For a spring sowing, dig in autumn and incorporate compost, well-rotted manure or other organic matter if the soil is poor. Potash is useful, so wood ash or comfrey leaves can be added where available. Apply a general-purpose fertilizer about a week before sowing.

After cropping, cut the stems at the base rather than pulling the whole plant if possible. This leaves the nitrogen-rich roots and nodules in the soil for the following crop, while the chopped stems can be composted.
Choose a warm, sunny, sheltered spot, such as a south-facing wall. Improve the bed with mature compost before planting. Use organic fertiliser only where soil fertility needs it.
Keep soil or compost evenly moist. Feed organically at the label rate once fruit starts to form. When the fourth truss on a cordon has set fruit, pinch out the main tip two leaves above it.

A dark, leathery patch at the flower end of the fruit results from insufficient calcium reaching developing tissue, often because root moisture fluctuates. Keep soil or compost evenly moist, especially as fruit swells; avoid root damage and excessive feeding. Diagnose soil conditions before adding lime or nutrients.

Potatoes prefer slightly acid conditions and should not be limed. Scab is encouraged by alkaline, dry soil; acidity reduces it. Potash is important for good crops, while nitrogen is useful but less critical where compost or manure has been added.

online.title: AHDB — Biological fixation of nitrogen by rhizobia
online.use: Root-nodule bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen; residues release nitrogen through mineralisation; contribution varies.

online.title: RHS — Organic matter: how to use in the garden
online.use: Photosynthesis, plant residues, decomposition and carbon dioxide; organic matter binds soil particles, retains nutrients and moisture; some forms last longer.

online.title: Garden Organic — The function of plant nutrients
online.use: Pages 2–4: organic and mineral phosphorus pools, availability and root function; potassium pools, water balance, fruit development, compost/comfrey recycling; other nutrients and uptake conditions.

online.title: RHS — How plants absorb nutrients
online.use: All plants need nutrients; nitrogen supports leafy growth, phosphorus roots, potassium fruiting; carbon comes from air.

online.title: RHS — Seaweed products
online.use: Seaweed provides potassium and trace elements; most soils have adequate micronutrients. Collection needs permission. Amounts are variable, so no complete-feed guarantee.

online.title: Garden Organic — Growing comfrey
online.use: Permanent undisturbed patch; let plants establish before regular cutting.

online.title: Garden Organic — Comfrey harvesting and use
online.use: Leaves can be mixed into compost to recycle their nutrients.

online.title: RHS — Three ways to use comfrey
online.use: Bocking 14 and composting cut leaves: a compact useful method without a liquid-feed recipe.

online.title: RHS — Leafmould
online.use: Leafmould is chiefly a soil conditioner; do not assume nutritional equivalence to mixed compost or manure.

online.title: RHS — Wood ash: using in the garden
online.use: Limited ash use, untreated timber, winter timing, avoid alkaline soil and potato beds.

editorialDecisions: Use N/P/K plus one micronutrient row, as requested; crop examples are benefits, not exclusive requirements.
Keep nitrogen fixation distinct from recycling: some residue nitrogen becomes available on decay. No yield or complete-feed promise.
Replace theoretical carbon loop with the practical carbon/organic-matter/humus relationship in the compost example.
Comfrey appears as a usable short method in the table, without pointing to a nonexistent guide.
John’s surface seaweed method takes precedence over RHS digging instructions. Do not repeat broad universal-fertiliser claims.
